text: All right. Good afternoon. I call the May 21st, 2026, meeting of the Student Services Committee to order. I am John Pepper. I am the chair of this committee, and joining me are my colleagues, Ms. April Chandler, school board chair of the Algonkian District, and Ms. Carrie Labelle of the Catoctin District.

We will begin our meeting with public comment, of which there is none. So we will move to the approval of the minutes. We have two sets of minutes to approve, the minutes of the April 16th, 2026, Student Services Committee meeting and the April 23rd, 2026, Student Services work session. And I will entertain a motion to approve those minutes. Ms. Chandler?

I move that we approve the draft minutes for the April 16th, 2026, Student Services Committee meeting and the April 23rd, 2026, Student Services work session. Is there a second? I second. Thank you, Ms. Labelle. That motion has been made by Ms. Chandler and seconded by Ms. Labelle. Is there any discussion? Seeing none, all of those in favor of approving both the minutes from the April 16th, 2026, Student

Services Committee meeting and the April 23rd, 2026, Student Services Committee work session, say aye. Aye. Aye. That motion has passed unanimously. I want to make a note for those of you who are looking at the agenda for our meeting online, that you will see a new item in the agenda. It is item 4.01 under a section called Presentation. That is not an item for information, discussion, or action. Instead, it is a placeholder so that those individuals who are viewing

our meeting can view the same PowerPoint presentation that we are all viewing. You will all be able to see that in future meetings, but we are actually going to skip over that and move to five, which is our action items. We have one action item on the agenda tonight. It is revised policy 8250 on bullying prevention and education. Do I have a motion for this item? Ms. Chandler?

I move that the Student Services Committee approves revised policy 8250, bullying prevention and education, and sends it to the full board as an information item. Thank you, Ms. Chandler. Is there a second? I second. Thank you, Ms. Labelle. That motion has been made by Ms. Chandler and seconded by Ms. Labelle. Is there any discussion among committee members? Ms. Chandler?

I was thinking. I saw you thinking, so yes, Ms. Chandler. Okay. Thank you, Chair Pepper. I have some questions. Could we discuss the use of the words systemic and chronic, and what those definition means, and if there is a legal definition or a broadly understood definition? I looked at the Virginia Code and didn't see anything that clearly stood out. Are those concepts that are clearly

understood by-educators and LCPS employees. Yes. So good afternoon. Thank you. That definition is from the state, from VDOE, and systemic means is this widespread, and then chronic is, is it ongoing? Oftentimes, we have students or parents who often use the term bullying when it's really peer conflict, or just interactions that raise some

concerns. So we really want to be clear that it has to be something that's happening on an ongoing basis. That's very helpful, and I appreciate the clarification that those are defined terms that are established by the VDOE. Mm-hmm. Is it appropriate in that same vein to look at the term ordinary teasing, which is on line 12? And what do you mean by looking at that term? Is that an- Like from teasing or peer conflict?

Well, so I'm curious if that is a more subjective term or if it's something that's clearly defined and understood by educators to mean something specific. Yes, so we do trainings on bullying prevention and intervention for our administrators and our school-based staff on how to respond to them, which does include the difference within the different categories. So could you give me an example of ordinary teasing? I don't want to play with you- Okay

... today. You can't sit with me at lunch versus every day, someone is being called a name over and over again by the same child. But within the supports that we provide to our educators, that is something that is completely understood and is not subjective. Absolutely. Okay. Thank you. That's great clarification. And then I was curious, in looking at some of the other policies that relate to

bullying in other jurisdictions, I know we changed our language based on suggestions that came in around cyberbullying. Mm-hmm. And I'm wondering if there's a need to capture the parameters and had to sort of entertain the idea of if do we need to define why we have the ability to discipline students when cyberbullying could occur outside of school? I believe we do

define that, and our administrators are aware that things outside of the school that impact the regular school day with peers, we do have jurisdiction to then respond and provide interventions as well as discipline. Is it typical for us to discipline students when cyberbullying is occurring between students and students who are perhaps in the same spaces during the school day, but the cyberbullying is occurring through devices while students are at home?

Yeah, and I think that would be part of the investigation that was done, and it depends on what type of cyberbullying and what that looks like. Sometimes there's threats, and then the school is then made aware of that, so we have our response, which could result in discipline. But the typical response is an intervention. So if we're made aware by a parent or one of the students in the school, we would start that investigation as soon as possible and inform all the parents that this allegation has been made and

provide supports to all parties. Well, thank you. You're welcome. That was really helpful. Ms. Lavelle. I'd like to add that those points that you just brought up, Ms. Chandler, about the bullying, that is all covered in the SBAC policies. It defines them. It says how they're handled. So they really are there. But the other thing that we do in many of our SBAC policies

and that we've done before in student services, is we offer a definition of what the different things are before we get into it. So I think that if we have very clear definitions in the beginning of our policy, especially if we're talking about, what were the two you had? Sy- Oh, systemic and chronic ... systemic and chronic. That could be helpful, and also a definition of teasing.

And it's not just for the teachers. It's for parents that tend to look these things up and then bring them back to us through SBAC saying, "Well, you didn't tell us what they were," or, "This wasn't clear." So that might be a good thing to add those particular definitions in there. Thank you. Absolutely. And one of the things that we do, whenever there's been a report, is we send a letter to the parents, which is a requirement within 24 hours. And within that, we include information

and resources which help define the difference between teasing, peer conflict, harassment, and also bullying. Okay. Anything else? Okay, so I have a few things, and they really came from some of the feedback that our community and some of our groups have put in here. The first is on line 86, where it is talking about,

actually now it's on 85, but it says, "Bullying prevention intervention programming should include evidence-based curricula practices and strategies." Just changing the word should to shall. Seems like it would be more fitting. Do we need to make a motion to do that as an amendment? I think we probably do. So I am going to make a motion to change on

85 the word should to shall. Do I have a second? Second. And Ms. Chandler has seconded. Is there any discussion on that? All right. All of those in favor of changing the word of line 85 from should to shall, please say aye. Aye. Ms. Chandler, do you have a question? Well, I'm wondering if we need to... Sorry. In looking at the following paragraphs- Mm-hmm

... I'm wondering then if we need to follow a consistent pattern. We do need to follow a consistent pattern. Okay. So I was going to go through it, and we can do these one at a time. So the next- Okay ... location, oh, now I've got to figure out where the next shall is. Could be 93. 93? Yes. And then 110. 93 and 110. Is there any others that we see as we scroll down here? No.

So that amendment passes

unanimously. There were a couple of other ones that I did want to make note of, and one is on lines 35 and 36. I did the easy ones first. On lines 35 and 36, one of our groups has noted that it's in conflict with lines 11, the definition of lines, it's actually 10 and 11,

that bullying is repeated over time or causes severe emotional trauma, and it's inconsistent because on lines 35, we just need to change the definition to match the other one. So on line 34, it's bullying is any unwanted, repeated, written, verbal, or physical behavior, including life-threatening, insulting, or dehumanizing gesture,

and take out the part that ending it after the word humiliation on line 37. So taking out the part that says, "and which unreasonably interferes with the school performance or participation of others." Okay. Ms. Chandler. Well, I was curious and would love to hear from staff if there's this particular reason why the language is different and if I could get some

clarification about how those definitions were pulled in the first place. One is from the state, and one was LCPS's definition within number two, but I do agree that there is a little bit of a contradiction there- Mm-hmm ... because it doesn't have to be repeated if it causes trauma. Right. So we can change that- Okay ... to be consistent. So if we remove those last sentences, right? The and which.

Anything beyond and which. Okay. Basically, it broadens it enough that it encompasses all forms. I believe it broadens it enough that it encompasses all forms of bullying. So we have to make a motion on that too, don't we? All right. So I'm going to move, and my computer is jumping around because it needs a restart, but I'm going to move that we eliminate the rest of the sentence on line 37 and line 38, starting with and which, and reads, "And which unreasonably

interferes with the school performance or participation of others." Is there a second? Thanks. Ms. LaBelle? Second. Second. Is there any further discussion among committee members? Okay, seeing none, all those in favor of removing the remainder of line 37, starting with and which on line 38, please say aye. Aye. Aye. Aye. So that passes unanimously. The other question I have

is on right about the same thing. It's going back to line 86, 87. This is not an amendment. It's actually on line 91 now, in the red line version. It says, "Records are to be kept and collected and the data analyzed semi-annually." Who is expected to analyze that data semi-annually? So each of our schools has a bullying prevention coordinator- Okay

... that is appointed by the administrator. Typically, it is the administrator. So we do collect that data. And we do have that not only with the discipline incidents but also with restorative practices. And we make sure that we are analyzing that data to see the instances that are occurring in our school division. Okay. Is it possible to add the line, "by the bullying prevention coordinator," after the word semi-annually, just to ensure that there's actually a

person tasked with analyzing this data? The bullying prevention coordination actually falls to central office, and then there's the coordinator, so would it make more sense to say at the division level? Or would you like it to say something around a coordinator at the school? I don't know if it's at the school level, but I feel like there has to be... So when you say at the division level, right? Mm-hmm. And I know it'll come to your office, and I know you guys are excellent and someone

will do it, but I really think it should be tasked to a specific person because of how important this is. So maybe we say both, at the school level and division level. Because I don't know that the coordinator is necessarily the one that's going to analyze the data, because it might be the administrator, it might be a designee. Right. With oversight from central office, so at the school level with-

And... Right. So my concern is it gets tasked to someone who isn't there. Right. Or it gets tasked to an administrator and no one has this specific task on their plate, so it just falls by the wayside.So, I actually would be okay with leaving it as is- Okay ... with the vagueness of it, just to ensure that it gets done. But with possibly revisiting to ensure that it does get done to all of our sites. Right. Absolutely.

we're bringing this policy to you as at least a majority of you have sat on appeal hearings for late requests received through policy 8160, which allows for the surveying of families for rezone students at either level. But my clarification even on this is that we're proposing a time limit

to receive late requests. It's not a time limit for appeals. So if I may speak to this item and offer that on line 67, and I've run this by Ms. Richardson before I said this out loud, if we create a new item number C3, that would read, "Late request received by

staff," and then take the added text that's on line 71 through 73. "Late requests received by staff, or must be received by staff within 60 calendar days of the school board action granting permission to those students whose parents or legal guardians requested an exception through the survey process." We want to limit the window with late requests.

Similar to policy 8155 that provides a limit for special permission requests. There's a cutoff. Then, the new item four would be line 68 through 70 as altered. "Staff decisions may be appealed to the school board following procedures of School Board Policy 2350, Appeal to Administrative Decisions." As you're aware, we have had in

excess of 30 late requests that have been appealed to the board. We have received others, but parents didn't take that additional step. This is the first time that we have been unable to approve, from a staff perspective, the requests that were received because all of the high schools were already at capacity based on policy 8155. So that was our reason for denial. As we continue to

review attendance zones over the coming years, that will not necessarily be tied to the opening of new schools. There is a possibility that staff would again deny late requests for parents who were initially surveyed but chose not to respond at that time. So, we're just proposing a 60 calendar day that gives the opportunity if a board were to review survey requests in December,

close for winter break, it still gives families two months basically to realize they've missed the survey period, but it doesn't continue to receive late requests into May and June as schools are trying to schedule, schools are staffing. So, I apologize that I'm not tracking with what was in the item and that I've pivoted on you, but I'm happy to answer questions specific to this.

Committee members, do you have questions for Ms. Tate or anyone else in the committee? Okay. Anybody? All right. Then I will happily answer questions on this. So right now, a survey goes out to any parent who has had their school zone changed based on rezoning, and they have a certain amount of time to respond to the survey, and if they

respond to the survey and they're within all the confines put in place, their requests are 100% automatically granted. Is that correct? We survey all families with students who- Mm-hmm ... fit in the parameter, and then we report back to the school board with those survey responsesWith the exception of one time that I recall, the board has approved those. Okay. But it's not an automatic necessarily.

The board with the Dulles South actually requested that we survey all the rising sophomores and rising juniors- Mm-hmm ... which wasn't part of policy. So they're not automatically approved, no, sir, but we do report to the board for their action. And I remember we did something with Madison's Trust, I believe, at one of the board meetings recently that was the same situation.

Okay, and then if parents, for whatever reason, or families, for whatever reason, have missed that window, and this is what we've sat on, then they can appeal individually through Policy 2350 to get a hearing in front of the board for approval. Is that correct? That is correct, if staff denies the request. Okay. Yes, sir. And there is no time limit currently on that? No, sir. Okay. The only concern I would have on all of this is

just to make sure that if a family does not return a survey, that we are working to contact them in some way just to do that-- If we're going to put a timeframe on it, because I will tell you, I think we got an email yesterday- Mm-hmm ... from a family, as a whole board, that missed the window. Or at least I did . And it seemed very late, and I was like, "This seems incredibly late." Just to make

sure that we just do one more round of like, "Hey, we didn't get something from you guys. Are you sure you're comfortable with your choice that your student is now going to attend school Y instead of their current school X?" Yes, sir, we can certainly do that. In our survey process, which typically runs a few weeks at least- Mm-hmm ... sometimes a month, we send reminder emails each week.

But yes, sir, we can certainly do that, and we have said in the survey, if you intend for your student to proceed to the school that will serve your residence, you do not have to respond. But we will endeavor to be more outreach. I appreciate that, because I think that's where the big-- And it's not 2002.

And we will do the public outreach community as part of the process, and then, yes, thank you. Thank you so much, Ms. Tate. All right. Moving on to our next and last information item. It's item 6.02, revised policy 5340, safe and supportive removal of students. This has also gone through several work sessions. And with that, Ms. Richardson, the floor is yours. Thank you, and good afternoon. So as a reminder, we have

had two scheduled work sessions, the first being on March 25th, the second being on April 23rd, in collaboration with representation from our board advisory groups. So we had SEAC, MSAC, GAC, and LEAF representation at our work sessions. So from the first work session, you will recall we divided the policy into sections. So we did the first four sections

in March, and some of the observations were: Let's focus on clarity. Let's be consistent with language throughout. Let's make sure we emphasize the need for de-escalation strategies first. The policy language was feeling a little punitive, more like discipline. Then the impact really wanted to be clear on documentation and transparency in reporting to families,

working to really build a shared understanding. There were some concerns about misuse or overuse of a safe and supportive removal, and then, of course, the consistency in implementation. Some of the recommendations coming out of the first work session on the first four sections of the policy were to clarify the criteria for use. Again, documentation and monitoring, making sure that we

provided additional clarity on the prohibited practices, and then when it came time for us to do professional learning should this policy be approved, making sure that it was scenario-based and making sure that our staff members and administrators get a chance to really role-play and work through some of the scenarios that they might encounter. Okay. In our April work session, we got a lot more information back, and so I'll just highlight. So observations,

the key terms were still not consistently defined throughout the policy. Roles and responsibilities needed to be clarified. We talked about timelines, the requirements for documentation and meetings, and also, making sure that the policy provided clarity on what the expectations were for re-entry back into the classroom or educational setting in which the student had been removed.

And then also making sure that we work on defining accountability. The impactWe wanted to make sure that we were filing these documents correctly, that we provided clarity on really who is the owner of these documents and how are they going to be maintained, access to this information, making sure that we are monitoring the amount of instructional time that students are missing.

Some feedback was that the processes could be subjective, and so that could increase the possibility for distrust, some fractured relationships between schools and families. And then certainly, it was recognized by our work session participants that this is going to be a heavy lift on staff and administrators with the documentation process.

So some of the recommendations coming out were just making sure that we tighten up that documentation process as much as we can so that it is accurately indicating the supports that we need to provide to that student, but then also making it a user-friendly format for our staff members. Make sure that we're adding those clear qualifiers, that we're defining those responsibilities and timelines, that we're providing clarity in our

operational processes, and that, again, we focus on that re-entry criteria so that students are not removed from the setting longer than what they need be. So you will see that we have completely overhauled the language in our policy. So, there was lots of feedback from our tabletop groups that that first paragraph,

that purpose, really had more of a negative tone. So staff have definitely tried to focus more on dignity, safety, and well-being, and not so much on that behavioral impact as it's taking place. And so in your documents, you should see the draft of the policy before our work sessions, and then what's in our slides is the outcome of our work sessions.

You can see for definitions, we did remove isolation and exclusion, and we did also add a definition for trained staff. There was lots of feedback on, "So what does a staff member mean? What does that mean? Is it a substitute? Is it a parent volunteer?" And so we have provided a definition for what trained staff are. Under conditions for use, we have added additional language

and focus on de-escalation and strategies to support students with self-regulation before the implementation of a safe and supportive removal to a designated supportive area. Expectations for professional learning, we flip-flopped some of the sections of the policy. There was lots of feedback on it's not quite flowing correctly. So for the professional

learning for staff, expectations have been defined there. We've also maintained that parent notification piece, and we also provided some clarity. There was lots of feedback on if a student is already eligible under the IDEA or ADA, and their educational planning teams have determined that some type of removal or support with self-regulation is

required, and the parent has signed for consent to implementation, that notification is not necessarily required in those instances. So we have captured that feedback. The documentation requirements, of course, date, time, duration, reason for action, the description of the events leading up to. There was a lot of focus on are we really being thoughtful about the aspects of what is happening

prior to us having to remove a student from that setting. And so in our documentation, we're making sure that there is a spot for that to be clearly outlined so that when we have our meeting to debrief and process, we're able to go back and really look at antecedents, behavior, and then that consequence, and how might we change some of those antecedents for this particular student.

Supervision and support of the student has remained somewhat the same. Review and monitoring, and then, of course, we kept the accountability aspect. Thank you, Ms. Richardson. Sure. So I appreciate having the opportunity to reflect on staff's position, but that is something that I'll be mulling over- Okay ... before we move forward.
